# Simultaneous Localization and Mapping {#sec-slam}

Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) estimates the robot trajectory and the map at the same time:

$$
p(\mathbf{x}_{1:k}, \mathbf{m} \mid \mathbf{z}_{1:k}, \mathbf{u}_{1:k}).
$$

The problem is hard because localization needs a map, while mapping needs a pose estimate. The usual joke is that SLAM is a chicken-and-egg problem. The less funny version is that a wrong data association can quietly poison the map and then use that poisoned map to justify future wrong poses.

This chapter gives a broad view of EKF-SLAM, FastSLAM, and GraphSLAM, but it goes deepest on FastSLAM because that is the implementation target for the Victoria Park project [@Montemerlo2002FastSLAM; @Thrun2004FastSLAM]. Throughout, $\mathbf{x}_k = [x_k, y_k, \theta_k]^T$ is the planar robot pose, $\boldsymbol{\ell}_j$ is the position of landmark $j$, and the map is $\mathbf{m} = \{\boldsymbol{\ell}_1, \ldots, \boldsymbol{\ell}_N\}$. Because $N$ counts landmarks, the number of particles is $M$.

## Online SLAM and Full SLAM {#sec-slam-online-slam-full}

**Online SLAM** estimates only the current robot pose and the map:

$$
p(\mathbf{x}_k, \mathbf{m} \mid \mathbf{z}_{1:k}, \mathbf{u}_{1:k}).
$$

**Full SLAM** estimates the whole trajectory and the map:

$$
p(\mathbf{x}_{1:k}, \mathbf{m} \mid \mathbf{z}_{1:k}, \mathbf{u}_{1:k}).
$$

Filtering methods such as EKF-SLAM and FastSLAM are usually presented as online algorithms. GraphSLAM and factor-graph methods are usually presented as full-trajectory smoothing algorithms. FastSLAM sits in between: each particle carries a whole path hypothesis, but the filter only ever moves forward in time.

## EKF-SLAM in One Page {#sec-slam-ekf-slam-one}

EKF-SLAM puts the robot pose and every landmark into one state vector and runs an ordinary EKF (@sec-ekf) on it. For a planar robot and $N$ point landmarks the state has $3 + 2N$ entries:

$$
\mathbf{y} =
\begin{bmatrix}
\mathbf{x} \\ \boldsymbol{\ell}_1 \\ \vdots \\ \boldsymbol{\ell}_N
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Its covariance splits into robot, map, and cross blocks,

$$
\mathbf{P} =
\begin{bmatrix}
\mathbf{P}_{xx} & \mathbf{P}_{xm} \\
\mathbf{P}_{mx} & \mathbf{P}_{mm}
\end{bmatrix},
$$

and it is dense. Those cross-correlations are not decorative: they are how the filter remembers that landmark uncertainty and robot uncertainty came from the same observations. The compressed EKF work on Victoria Park is a useful historical reference for why managing this dense matrix became the practical bottleneck [@GuivantNebot2001CompressedEKFSLAM].

**Prediction.** Landmarks do not move, so only the robot block and the robot-map cross terms change. With $\mathbf{F} = \partial f / \partial \mathbf{x}$ and $\mathbf{L} = \partial f / \partial \mathbf{u}$ evaluated at the current estimate, and odometry noise $\mathbf{Q}_u$ entering through the inputs (@sec-kf-input-noise),

$$
\begin{aligned}
\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k|k-1} &= f(\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k-1|k-1}, \mathbf{u}_k), \\
\mathbf{P}_{xx} &\leftarrow \mathbf{F}\mathbf{P}_{xx}\mathbf{F}^T + \mathbf{L}\mathbf{Q}_u\mathbf{L}^T, \\
\mathbf{P}_{xm} &\leftarrow \mathbf{F}\mathbf{P}_{xm},
\qquad \mathbf{P}_{mx} = \mathbf{P}_{xm}^T, \\
\mathbf{P}_{mm} &\leftarrow \mathbf{P}_{mm}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-slam-ekf-predict}

The robot moved, so its correlation with each landmark is carried along by $\mathbf{F}$; the landmark block is untouched. Prediction costs $O(N)$.

**Update.** A range-bearing observation of landmark $j$ depends only on the robot pose and $\boldsymbol{\ell}_j$, so its Jacobian is zero except in two column blocks:

$$
\mathbf{H} =
\begin{bmatrix}
\mathbf{H}_x & \mathbf{0} & \cdots & \mathbf{0} & \mathbf{H}_\ell & \mathbf{0} & \cdots & \mathbf{0}
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Here $\mathbf{H}_x$ is the $2 \times 3$ pose Jacobian of @eq-measurement-models-range-bearing-H, and the $2 \times 2$ landmark Jacobian $\mathbf{H}_\ell$ is minus its first two columns. With the innovation's bearing component wrapped to $[-\pi, \pi)$, the update is the usual EKF update,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\boldsymbol{\nu} &= \mathbf{z} - h(\hat{\mathbf{x}}, \hat{\boldsymbol{\ell}}_j), \\
\mathbf{S} &= \mathbf{H}\mathbf{P}\mathbf{H}^T + \mathbf{R}, \\
\mathbf{K} &= \mathbf{P}\mathbf{H}^T\mathbf{S}^{-1}, \\
\hat{\mathbf{y}} &\leftarrow \hat{\mathbf{y}} + \mathbf{K}\boldsymbol{\nu}, \\
\mathbf{P} &\leftarrow \mathbf{P} - \mathbf{K}\mathbf{S}\mathbf{K}^T,
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-slam-ekf-update}

but the sparsity of $\mathbf{H}$ says a lot about where the work goes. $\mathbf{S}$ only involves the blocks $\mathbf{P}_{xx}$, $\mathbf{P}_{xj}$, and $\mathbf{P}_{jj}$, so it is cheap. $\mathbf{P}\mathbf{H}^T$ only uses the robot and landmark-$j$ columns of $\mathbf{P}$, but every row of it is generally nonzero, so the gain is dense: one observation of one tree nudges every landmark that is correlated with the robot. That is exactly how EKF-SLAM propagates a loop closure through the whole map. The bill arrives in the covariance update, where $\mathbf{K}\mathbf{S}\mathbf{K}^T$ is a full $(3+2N) \times (3+2N)$ outer product. Every observation costs $O(N^2)$ time, and storing $\mathbf{P}$ costs $O(N^2)$ memory. Use the Joseph form (@sec-kf-joseph-form) if you care about keeping $\mathbf{P}$ symmetric and positive definite, which you do.

**Augmentation.** A new landmark comes from the inverse observation model,

$$
\boldsymbol{\ell} = g(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{z}) =
\begin{bmatrix}
x + r\cos(\theta + \beta) \\
y + r\sin(\theta + \beta)
\end{bmatrix},
$$

with Jacobians with respect to the pose and the measurement

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{G}_x &=
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 0 & -r\sin(\theta+\beta) \\
0 & 1 & r\cos(\theta+\beta)
\end{bmatrix}, \\
\mathbf{G}_z &=
\begin{bmatrix}
\cos(\theta+\beta) & -r\sin(\theta+\beta) \\
\sin(\theta+\beta) & r\cos(\theta+\beta)
\end{bmatrix}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The state grows by two entries, and the covariance by a new row and column of blocks:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{P}_{\ell\ell} &= \mathbf{G}_x\mathbf{P}_{xx}\mathbf{G}_x^T + \mathbf{G}_z\mathbf{R}\mathbf{G}_z^T, \\
\mathbf{P}_{\ell x} &= \mathbf{G}_x\mathbf{P}_{xx}, \\
\mathbf{P}_{\ell m} &= \mathbf{G}_x\mathbf{P}_{xm}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-slam-ekf-augment}

The new landmark inherits the robot's uncertainty and, through it, a correlation with every landmark the robot is already correlated with. Dropping the cross terms would declare the new tree independent of the robot that just measured it, an overconfident lie that the filter would happily believe forever.

**Consistency.** Julier and Uhlmann showed with a deceptively simple counterexample that the EKF-SLAM covariance can shrink below anything the measurements justify, so the filter becomes inconsistent, most visibly in heading [@julierUhlmann2001slam]. Huang, Mourikis, and Roumeliotis traced the cause to observability [@huang2010]. Planar SLAM cannot observe the global position and orientation of the whole map-plus-robot picture: three directions are unobservable. Because the EKF evaluates its Jacobians at different estimates at different times, its *linearized* system appears to observe the global heading, and the filter acquires heading information that does not exist. Their first-estimates Jacobian (FEJ) EKF evaluates each Jacobian at the first estimate of the state it involves, and their observability-constrained (OC) EKF chooses linearization points that keep the correct unobservable subspace. Both cost essentially nothing extra and fix most of the overconfidence.

So EKF-SLAM is conceptually elegant and historically important, and its correlations do real work, but $O(N^2)$ per observation and linearization-induced overconfidence are why it is not the project backend.

## FastSLAM: The Project Backend {#sec-slam-fastslam-project-backend}

FastSLAM uses a Rao-Blackwellized particle filter (@sec-pf-rao-blackwellized) [@Montemerlo2002FastSLAM]. Let $n_k$ be the *correspondence* of the measurement at time $k$: the index of the landmark that produced it. The key factorization holds *given the correspondences*:

$$
\begin{aligned}
p(\mathbf{x}_{1:k}, \mathbf{m} \mid \mathbf{z}_{1:k}, \mathbf{u}_{1:k}, n_{1:k})
={}& p(\mathbf{x}_{1:k} \mid \mathbf{z}_{1:k}, \mathbf{u}_{1:k}, n_{1:k}) \\
&\times \prod_{j=1}^{N} p(\boldsymbol{\ell}_j \mid \mathbf{x}_{1:k}, \mathbf{z}_{1:k}, n_{1:k}).
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-slam-fastslam-factorization}

Here is why. Condition on the whole path. By Bayes' rule, and with independent landmark priors,

$$
p(\mathbf{m} \mid \mathbf{x}_{1:k}, \mathbf{z}_{1:k}, n_{1:k})
\propto
\prod_{j=1}^{N} p(\boldsymbol{\ell}_j)
\prod_{\tau=1}^{k} p(\mathbf{z}_\tau \mid \mathbf{x}_\tau, \boldsymbol{\ell}_{n_\tau}).
$$

Each measurement likelihood involves exactly one landmark, the one named by $n_\tau$. Group the factors by landmark and the posterior splits into $N$ independent pieces, each of which is a small estimation problem for a fixed point seen from known sensor positions. That is precisely what a $2 \times 2$ EKF solves.

Now drop the correspondences. The likelihood of one measurement becomes a mixture over which landmark produced it,

$$
p(\mathbf{z}_\tau \mid \mathbf{x}_\tau, \mathbf{m})
=
\sum_{j} P(n_\tau = j)\, p(\mathbf{z}_\tau \mid \mathbf{x}_\tau, \boldsymbol{\ell}_j),
$$

and a product of sums does not split into a product over landmarks. Unknown association couples every landmark to every other. FastSLAM's way out is to let each particle carry its own correspondence history $n_{1:k}^{[i]}$ along with its path $\mathbf{x}_{1:k}^{[i]}$. Inside a particle the correspondences are "known" and @eq-slam-fastslam-factorization holds, so the particles sample paths and associations jointly. That is why different particles may disagree about which tree is which, and why a wrong association need not be fatal as long as some particle got it right. @sec-slam-association is about making those per-particle decisions well.

FastSLAM therefore represents:

- the robot path and the association history with particles;
- each landmark inside each particle with a small EKF;
- the particle weight with the likelihood of the observations (@sec-slam-landmark-weighting).

For Victoria Park, each particle carries its own hypothesis about the vehicle path through the park and its own tree map.

### Particle State

A practical particle contains:

```text
pose:          [x, y, theta]
trajectory:    previous poses, for plotting and for the path posterior
landmarks:     dictionary landmark_id -> LandmarkEKF (mean, covariance,
               hit count, last scan seen; tentative until confirmed)
log_weight:    accumulated measurement log-likelihood
```

The per-landmark EKF state is only two-dimensional:

$$
\hat{\boldsymbol{\ell}}_j^{[i]} \in \mathbb{R}^{2},
\qquad
\mathbf{P}_j^{[i]} \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 2}.
$$

That is why FastSLAM is attractive for large landmark maps: $M$ particles times $N$ tiny filters, instead of one filter with a $(3+2N)^2$ covariance.

## A Small Range-Bearing World {#sec-slam-small-range-bearing}

Before working with the dataset, it helps to make the geometry concrete. The toy world below has three trees, a robot driving a gentle left-hand arc, and a 360-degree range-bearing sensor that sees from 1 m out to 8 m. (The minimum range is not decoration: the path passes within half a meter of the first tree, and a range-bearing EKF fed a 30 cm range with 25 cm of noise is a filter being asked to divide by nearly zero.) The true robot executes the commanded speed and turn rate *plus noise*, so the odometry handed to the filter is wrong in the same way real odometry is wrong. Nobody tells the filter which measurement came from which tree.

::: {#fastslam-toy-world .cell execution_count=1}
``` {.python .cell-code}
import collections
import math

import numpy as np


def wrap_angle(angle):
    """Wrap an angle to [-pi, pi)."""
    return (angle + np.pi) % (2.0 * np.pi) - np.pi


def predict_pose(pose, control, dt):
    """Planar unicycle motion model; control = [v, omega]."""
    x, y, theta = pose
    v, omega = control

    if abs(omega) < 1e-9:
        x = x + v * math.cos(theta) * dt
        y = y + v * math.sin(theta) * dt
    else:
        x = x + (v / omega) * (math.sin(theta + omega * dt) - math.sin(theta))
        y = y + (v / omega) * (-math.cos(theta + omega * dt) + math.cos(theta))

    theta = wrap_angle(theta + omega * dt)
    return np.array([x, y, theta], dtype=float)


def observe_landmark(pose, landmark_xy):
    """Range-bearing observation of one 2D landmark."""
    dx, dy = np.asarray(landmark_xy) - pose[:2]
    return np.array([
        math.hypot(dx, dy),
        wrap_angle(math.atan2(dy, dx) - pose[2]),
    ])


true_landmarks = np.array([
    [4.0, 1.0],
    [7.0, -1.5],
    [10.0, 2.0],
])

R = np.diag([0.25**2, np.deg2rad(2.0)**2])     # measurement noise: range [m], bearing [rad]
Q_u = np.diag([0.05**2, np.deg2rad(1.0)**2])   # odometry noise on [v, omega] per 1 s step
COMMAND = np.array([0.8, 0.05])                # commanded [m/s, rad/s]
MIN_RANGE, MAX_RANGE = 1.0, 8.0                # [m]; the sensor sees all the way around


def simulate_run(seed, *, steps=12, control_covariance=Q_u, measurement_covariance=R):
    """Simulate the toy world: true poses and unlabeled range-bearing scans.

    The true robot executes COMMAND plus noise drawn from `control_covariance`,
    so the odometry the filter receives (COMMAND) is imperfect. Each scan lists
    noisy [range, bearing] pairs for every tree between MIN_RANGE and MAX_RANGE.
    """
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    pose = np.zeros(3)
    true_poses, scans = [], []
    for _ in range(steps):
        executed = COMMAND + rng.multivariate_normal(np.zeros(2), control_covariance)
        pose = predict_pose(pose, executed, dt=1.0)
        scan = []
        for landmark_xy in true_landmarks:
            z = observe_landmark(pose, landmark_xy)
            if MIN_RANGE < z[0] < MAX_RANGE:
                z = z + rng.multivariate_normal(np.zeros(2), measurement_covariance)
                z[1] = wrap_angle(z[1])
                scan.append(z)
        true_poses.append(pose.copy())
        scans.append(scan)
    return np.array(true_poses), scans


true_poses, scans = simulate_run(seed=4)
print(f"{len(scans)} scans; observations per scan: {[len(s) for s in scans]}")
print("first scan (range m, bearing rad):", np.round(scans[0], 3).tolist())
```

## Per-Landmark EKF {#sec-slam-per-landmark-ekf}

Each landmark EKF estimates a fixed point in the world. The robot pose is treated as known within a particle, which is the whole point of @eq-slam-fastslam-factorization. Initialization pushes the measurement noise through the inverse observation model, $\mathbf{P}_\ell = \mathbf{G}_z \mathbf{R} \mathbf{G}_z^T$; there is no $\mathbf{G}_x$ term because inside a particle the pose has no uncertainty to inherit. (@sec-slam-association-landmark-birth contrasts this with full EKF-SLAM initialization.)

::: {#landmark-ekf .cell execution_count=2}
``` {.python .cell-code}
LOG_2PI = math.log(2.0 * math.pi)


def gaussian_log_likelihood(nu, S):
    """log N(nu; 0, S) = -1/2 nu^T S^-1 nu - 1/2 log det(2 pi S)."""
    _, logdet = np.linalg.slogdet(S)
    return float(-0.5 * nu @ np.linalg.solve(S, nu) - 0.5 * (len(nu) * LOG_2PI + logdet))


class LandmarkEKF:
    """EKF for one 2D landmark, conditioned on one particle's path.

    Instances are treated as immutable values: `updated()` returns a new
    object instead of modifying this one. That is what lets resampled particles
    share landmarks safely (@sec-slam-why-fast).
    """

    __slots__ = ("mean", "covariance", "hits", "last_seen")

    def __init__(self, mean, covariance, hits=0, last_seen=0):
        self.mean = np.asarray(mean, dtype=float)
        self.covariance = np.asarray(covariance, dtype=float)
        self.hits = hits              # successful associations since birth
        self.last_seen = last_seen    # scan index of the latest association

    @classmethod
    def initialize(cls, pose, measurement, measurement_covariance, scan_index=0):
        """Initialize from one range-bearing observation (inverse model)."""
        r, bearing = measurement
        angle = pose[2] + bearing
        mean = np.array([
            pose[0] + r * math.cos(angle),
            pose[1] + r * math.sin(angle),
        ])
        # G_z = d(landmark) / d(range, bearing). The pose is known in a particle.
        G_z = np.array([
            [math.cos(angle), -r * math.sin(angle)],
            [math.sin(angle), r * math.cos(angle)],
        ])
        return cls(mean, G_z @ measurement_covariance @ G_z.T, 0, scan_index)

    def expected_measurement(self, pose):
        """Predicted [range, bearing] and the Jacobian H_l wrt the landmark."""
        dx, dy = self.mean - pose[:2]
        q = dx * dx + dy * dy
        r = math.sqrt(q)
        z_hat = np.array([r, wrap_angle(math.atan2(dy, dx) - pose[2])])
        H_l = np.array([
            [dx / r, dy / r],
            [-dy / q, dx / q],
        ])
        return z_hat, H_l

    def innovation(self, pose, measurement, measurement_covariance):
        """Innovation nu (bearing wrapped), H_l, and S = H_l P H_l^T + R."""
        z_hat, H_l = self.expected_measurement(pose)
        nu = np.asarray(measurement, dtype=float) - z_hat
        nu[1] = wrap_angle(nu[1])
        S = H_l @ self.covariance @ H_l.T + measurement_covariance
        return nu, H_l, S

    def updated(self, pose, measurement, measurement_covariance, scan_index=0):
        """Return the posterior landmark after one EKF update (Joseph form)."""
        nu, H_l, S = self.innovation(pose, measurement, measurement_covariance)
        K = np.linalg.solve(S, H_l @ self.covariance).T
        I_KH = np.eye(2) - K @ H_l
        covariance = (
            I_KH @ self.covariance @ I_KH.T
            + K @ measurement_covariance @ K.T
        )
        return LandmarkEKF(self.mean + K @ nu, covariance, self.hits + 1, scan_index)


pose = np.zeros(3)
first_observation = observe_landmark(pose, true_landmarks[0])
landmark = LandmarkEKF.initialize(pose, first_observation, R)
print("landmark mean:", landmark.mean)
print("landmark std devs [m]:", np.sqrt(np.diag(landmark.covariance)).round(3))
```

The Joseph-form covariance update is used here for the same reason it was used in @sec-kf-joseph-form: it is slightly more expensive and much less annoying. Notice the initial uncertainty: 0.25 m along the line of sight (the range noise) but only about 0.14 m across it (2 degrees at 4.1 m). Beyond about 7 m, where 2 degrees of bearing equals 25 cm, the ellipse turns the other way, and at the tens of meters typical of Victoria Park the bearing error dominates: new trees start out as long thin ellipses lying across the line of sight.

## Weighting Particles: Matched and New Landmarks {#sec-slam-landmark-weighting}

FastSLAM 1.0 samples each particle's new pose from the motion model, so by @eq-pf-bootstrap-weight its weight is multiplied by the likelihood of the scan given that particle's pose and map. For an observation matched to landmark $j$, integrate the uncertain landmark out. Linearizing $h$ about $\hat{\boldsymbol{\ell}}_j$ gives a Gaussian in the innovation,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\log \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\nu}; \mathbf{0}, \mathbf{S})
&=
-\tfrac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{\nu}^T\mathbf{S}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\nu}
-\tfrac{1}{2}\log\det(2\pi\mathbf{S}), \\
\mathbf{S} &= \mathbf{H}_\ell\mathbf{P}_j\mathbf{H}_\ell^T + \mathbf{R},
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-slam-matched-weight}

with the bearing component of $\boldsymbol{\nu}$ wrapped to $[-\pi, \pi)$. Both terms matter. The first rewards a small Mahalanobis distance. The second rewards a confident map: of two particles that explain the data equally well, the one with the tighter landmarks is the better hypothesis.

An observation that spawns a *new* landmark has no prediction to compare with, so there is no innovation to score. FastSLAM charges it a constant, the new-feature likelihood $p_0$ [@Montemerlo2003FastSLAM2; @ProbRob]:

$$
\log w^{[i]} \leftarrow \log w^{[i]} + \log p_0 .
$$

It is tempting to skip $p_0$ and simply leave the weight alone, which amounts to multiplying by one. Don't. @eq-slam-matched-weight is a probability *density* over measurement space, so it carries units, here $1/(\text{m}\cdot\text{rad})$, and its numerical value depends on them. Write ranges in centimeters instead of meters and every matched density is divided by 100 (the Jacobian of the unit change), while the Mahalanobis distances do not change at all. Leaving new-landmark particles alone means comparing those densities against an implicit 1, and *1 per what* is decided by whoever wrote the parser. In meters, the matched densities of the toy sensor are mostly larger than one, so the implicit choice mildly penalizes particles that spawn landmarks. In centimeters, they are mostly smaller than one, and the same code now rewards particles for inventing trees. A weighting rule that flips with your choice of units is not a rule.

So $p_0$ must itself be a density in the same units: the density of a measurement produced by something that is not in the particle's map. A natural choice treats such a measurement as equally likely anywhere in the sensor footprint,

$$
p_0 = \frac{1}{r_{\max}\, \Delta\beta},
$$ {#eq-slam-p0}

where $\Delta\beta$ is the field of view. For the toy sensor ($r_{\max} = 8$ m, $\Delta\beta = 2\pi$), $p_0 = 0.020\ \text{m}^{-1}\text{rad}^{-1}$. In centimeters it is $0.00020\ \text{cm}^{-1}\text{rad}^{-1}$: divided by 100, exactly like the matched densities, so every comparison is unit-invariant.

A useful sanity check is the Mahalanobis distance at which a well-mapped landmark ($\mathbf{S} \approx \mathbf{R}$) stops being a better explanation than "something new". Setting $\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\nu}; \mathbf{0}, \mathbf{R}) = p_0$ gives

$$
d^2_\times = -2 \log\!\left(2\pi\, p_0 \sqrt{\det \mathbf{R}}\right) \approx 13.6
$$

for the toy sensor, right next to the 99.9% chi-square value of 13.82 that the project uses as its birth gate (@sec-slam-association-landmark-birth). The gate and $p_0$ are two views of the same decision. For a different sensor, compute both and make sure they tell a consistent story.

This book uses one more rule: **every observation contributes exactly one factor to every particle's weight**, $\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\nu}; \mathbf{0}, \mathbf{S})$ if it updated a landmark and $p_0$ otherwise. "Otherwise" includes observations that a particle discards as ambiguous (@sec-slam-fastslam-algorithm): the particle could not explain them with its map, and charging nothing would reintroduce the units problem. Because every particle receives the same number of factors, adding a constant to all the factors of one observation shifts every log weight equally and disappears in normalization. One consequence is used in the experiment of @sec-slam-what-goes-wrong: running without $p_0$ with ranges in centimeters is *exactly* running with $p_0 = 100\ \text{m}^{-1}\text{rad}^{-1}$ in meters.

::: {#landmark-weighting-units .cell execution_count=3}

p0 = 1.0 / (MAX_RANGE * 2.0 * math.pi)          # [1 / (m rad)]
nu_m = np.array([0.30, np.deg2rad(1.5)])         # a typical matched innovation
S_m = 2.0 * R                                    # roughly a young landmark

to_cm = np.diag([100.0, 1.0])                    # range in cm, bearing still in rad
nu_cm, S_cm = to_cm @ nu_m, to_cm @ S_m @ to_cm.T

print(f"Mahalanobis d^2:  m: {nu_m @ np.linalg.solve(S_m, nu_m):.3f}   "
      f"cm: {nu_cm @ np.linalg.solve(S_cm, nu_cm):.3f}")
print(f"log N(nu; 0, S):  m: {gaussian_log_likelihood(nu_m, S_m):+.3f}   "
      f"cm: {gaussian_log_likelihood(nu_cm, S_cm):+.3f}   "
      f"(difference = log 100 = {math.log(100):.3f})")
print(f"log p0:           m: {math.log(p0):+.3f}   cm: {math.log(p0 / 100):+.3f}")

d2_crossover = -2.0 * math.log(2.0 * math.pi * p0 * math.sqrt(np.linalg.det(R)))
print(f"N(nu; 0, R) drops below p0 at d^2 = {d2_crossover:.1f}")

With the same innovation, the log-likelihood is $+1.7$ in meters and $-2.9$ in centimeters. Against an implicit $\log 1 = 0$, that match wins in one unit system and loses in the other. Against $\log p_0$, it wins by the same margin in both.

## FastSLAM Algorithm {#sec-slam-fastslam-algorithm}

For each scan $k$, and for each particle $i$:

1. **Predict.** Sample $\mathbf{x}_k^{[i]} \sim p(\mathbf{x}_k \mid \mathbf{x}_{k-1}^{[i]}, \mathbf{u}_k)$ by adding noise drawn from $\mathbf{Q}_u$ to the odometry and pushing it through the motion model.
2. **Associate**, inside the particle's own map (@sec-slam-association). Compute $d^2_{aj} = \boldsymbol{\nu}_{aj}^T\mathbf{S}_{aj}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\nu}_{aj}$ for every observation $a$ and landmark $j$. Match pairs with $d^2 < \chi^2_{2,0.95} = 5.99$ greedily in order of increasing $d^2$, and never let two observations of one scan update the same landmark (mutual exclusion). An unmatched observation spawns a *tentative* landmark only if $d^2 > \chi^2_{2,0.999} = 13.82$ for every existing landmark; otherwise it is ambiguous and is discarded.
3. **Update and weight.** A matched observation updates its landmark EKF and adds @eq-slam-matched-weight to the log weight. A new or discarded observation adds $\log p_0$.
4. **Manage tracks.** A tentative landmark becomes *confirmed* after three successful associations; a tentative landmark not seen again within a few scans is deleted.

Then, once per scan:

5. **Normalize** the log weights with log-sum-exp (@sec-pf-practical-implementation-considerations), remember the highest-weight particle, and **resample** (systematic, with the `cumulative[-1] = 1.0` guard of @sec-pf-resampling) when the effective sample size drops below half the particles:

$$
N_\text{eff} = \frac{1}{\sum_{i=1}^{M} \left(w^{[i]}\right)^2} < \frac{M}{2}.
$$

Resampling every step is usually too aggressive; resampling only when $N_\text{eff}$ drops preserves more particle diversity. The two-gate rule is the heart of the bookkeeping. One gate is not enough: with a single 95% gate, one correct re-observation in twenty fails it and spawns a duplicate tree, which over a few hundred observations is a forest. The band between the gates is where an honest filter says "I am not sure" and declines to touch the map.

CHI2_2DOF_95 = 5.991     # association gate
CHI2_2DOF_999 = 13.816   # birth gate
NEW, DISCARD = "new", "discard"


def two_gate_decisions(d2, landmark_ids, associate_gate, birth_gate, mutual_exclusion=True):
    """Decide each observation's fate from a (K x N) table of Mahalanobis distances.

    Observation a is matched to landmark j when d2[a, j] < associate_gate,
    greedily in order of increasing d2 and, with mutual exclusion, at most one
    observation per landmark per scan. An unmatched observation spawns a new
    landmark only if d2 > birth_gate for every existing landmark; otherwise it
    is ambiguous and is discarded.
    """
    num_obs = d2.shape[0]
    decisions = [None] * num_obs
    claimed = set()
    for a, col in sorted(zip(*np.nonzero(d2 < associate_gate)), key=lambda ac: d2[ac]):
        j = landmark_ids[col]
        if decisions[a] is None and (j not in claimed or not mutual_exclusion):
            decisions[a] = j
            claimed.add(j)
    for a in range(num_obs):
        if decisions[a] is None:
            far_from_all = d2.shape[1] == 0 or d2[a].min() > birth_gate
            decisions[a] = NEW if far_from_all else DISCARD
    return decisions


class FastSLAMParticle:
    """One FastSLAM particle: a pose history, a landmark map, and a log weight."""

    __slots__ = ("pose", "trajectory", "landmarks", "log_weight")

    def __init__(self, pose, trajectory=None, landmarks=None, log_weight=0.0):
        self.pose = np.asarray(pose, dtype=float)
        self.trajectory = [self.pose] if trajectory is None else trajectory
        self.landmarks = {} if landmarks is None else landmarks
        self.log_weight = log_weight

    def copy(self):
        """Copy-on-write copy: new containers, shared (immutable) landmarks."""
        return FastSLAMParticle(
            self.pose, list(self.trajectory), dict(self.landmarks), self.log_weight
        )


class FastSLAM:
    """FastSLAM 1.0 for range-bearing point landmarks with unknown association."""

    def __init__(
        self,
        num_particles,
        initial_pose,
        control_covariance,
        measurement_covariance,
        *,
        log_p0,
        associate_gate=CHI2_2DOF_95,
        birth_gate=CHI2_2DOF_999,
        confirm_hits=3,
        tentative_window=3,
        resample_fraction=0.5,
        mutual_exclusion=True,
        rng=None,
    ):
        self.particles = [FastSLAMParticle(initial_pose) for _ in range(num_particles)]
        self.control_covariance = np.asarray(control_covariance, dtype=float)
        self.R = np.asarray(measurement_covariance, dtype=float)
        self.log_p0 = log_p0
        self.associate_gate = associate_gate
        self.birth_gate = birth_gate
        self.confirm_hits = confirm_hits
        self.tentative_window = tentative_window
        self.resample_fraction = resample_fraction
        self.mutual_exclusion = mutual_exclusion
        self.rng = np.random.default_rng(0) if rng is None else rng
        self.scan_index = 0
        self.next_landmark_id = 0
        self.num_resamples = 0
        self.ess_history = []
        self.best_particle = self.particles[0]

    def step(self, control, dt, scan):
        self.predict(control, dt)
        self.update(scan)

    # -- 1. prediction: sample the motion model (the FastSLAM 1.0 proposal) ---
    def predict(self, control, dt):
        noise = self.rng.multivariate_normal(
            np.zeros(2), self.control_covariance, size=len(self.particles)
        )
        for particle, control_noise in zip(self.particles, noise):
            particle.pose = predict_pose(particle.pose, control + control_noise, dt)
            particle.trajectory.append(particle.pose)

    # -- 2. association inside one particle ----------------------------------
    def associate(self, particle, scan):
        ids = list(particle.landmarks)
        d2 = np.empty((len(scan), len(ids)))
        cache = {}
        for col, j in enumerate(ids):
            for a, z in enumerate(scan):
                nu, _, S = particle.landmarks[j].innovation(particle.pose, z, self.R)
                d2[a, col] = nu @ np.linalg.solve(S, nu)
                cache[a, j] = (nu, S)
        decisions = two_gate_decisions(
            d2, ids, self.associate_gate, self.birth_gate, self.mutual_exclusion
        )
        return decisions, cache

    # -- 3. and 4. update, weight, and manage tracks -------------------------
    def update(self, scan):
        self.scan_index += 1
        for particle in self.particles:
            decisions, cache = self.associate(particle, scan)
            for a, (z, decision) in enumerate(zip(scan, decisions)):
                if decision == NEW:
                    particle.landmarks[self.next_landmark_id] = LandmarkEKF.initialize(
                        particle.pose, z, self.R, self.scan_index
                    )
                    self.next_landmark_id += 1
                    particle.log_weight += self.log_p0
                elif decision == DISCARD:
                    particle.log_weight += self.log_p0
                else:
                    nu, S = cache[a, decision]
                    particle.log_weight += gaussian_log_likelihood(nu, S)
                    particle.landmarks[decision] = particle.landmarks[decision].updated(
                        particle.pose, z, self.R, self.scan_index
                    )
            self._delete_stale_tentative(particle)
        self._finish_update()

    def _delete_stale_tentative(self, particle):
        stale = [
            j for j, lm in particle.landmarks.items()
            if lm.hits < self.confirm_hits
            and self.scan_index - lm.last_seen > self.tentative_window
        ]
        for j in stale:
            del particle.landmarks[j]

    # -- 5. normalize, remember the best particle, maybe resample -------------
    def _finish_update(self):
        log_w = np.array([p.log_weight for p in self.particles])
        peak = log_w.max()
        log_w = log_w - (peak + math.log(np.sum(np.exp(log_w - peak))))
        for particle, lw in zip(self.particles, log_w):
            particle.log_weight = float(lw)

        weights = np.exp(log_w)
        ess = 1.0 / np.sum(weights**2)
        self.ess_history.append(ess)
        # Keep a handle on the best particle *before* resampling equalizes weights.
        self.best_particle = self.particles[int(np.argmax(weights))]
        if ess < self.resample_fraction * len(self.particles):
            self.resample(weights)

    def resample(self, weights):
        """Systematic resampling with the cumulative[-1] = 1 guard."""
        n = len(self.particles)
        positions = (self.rng.random() + np.arange(n)) / n
        cumulative = np.cumsum(weights)
        cumulative[-1] = 1.0
        indexes = np.searchsorted(cumulative, positions)
        self.particles = [self.particles[i].copy() for i in indexes]
        for particle in self.particles:
            particle.log_weight = -math.log(n)
        self.num_resamples += 1

    def weights(self):
        return np.exp([p.log_weight for p in self.particles])

    def effective_sample_size(self):
        return float(1.0 / np.sum(self.weights() ** 2))

    def estimated_pose(self):
        weights = self.weights()
        poses = np.array([p.pose for p in self.particles])
        xy = weights @ poses[:, :2]
        theta = math.atan2(weights @ np.sin(poses[:, 2]), weights @ np.cos(poses[:, 2]))
        return np.array([xy[0], xy[1], theta])

    def best_map(self):
        """Confirmed landmarks of the highest-weight particle (pre-resampling)."""
        return {
            j: lm.mean.copy()
            for j, lm in self.best_particle.landmarks.items()
            if lm.hits >= self.confirm_hits
        }

## Data Association Inside FastSLAM {#sec-slam-data-association-inside}

In EKF-SLAM, there is one global association decision for each measurement. In FastSLAM, each particle makes its own decision with its own pose and map, so different particles can preserve different hypotheses while the pose is uncertain. This is one of FastSLAM's real advantages, and it is the second half of the factorization argument: particles sample the association history along with the path.

For one particle and one scan, the project spec is the procedure coded above:

1. predict the measurement of every nearby landmark and compute the innovation, with the bearing wrapped;
2. compute the Mahalanobis distance $d^2$ of every observation-landmark pair;
3. match pairs below the 95% gate, smallest $d^2$ first, at most one observation per landmark;
4. spawn a tentative landmark only if an unmatched observation is beyond the 99.9% gate for *every* landmark, and discard it otherwise;
5. charge $\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\nu}; \mathbf{0}, \mathbf{S})$ for matches and $p_0$ for everything else.

The gates matter. A gate that is too tight creates duplicate trees. A gate that is too loose fuses distinct trees. Both failure modes are visible in the final map. @sec-slam-association develops the gating statistics, a worked gate-sensitivity example on closely spaced trees, joint compatibility for when innovations are correlated, optimal one-to-one assignment, and association sampling.

## Why "Fast": Sharing Landmarks Between Particles {#sec-slam-why-fast}

The name is not about the per-landmark EKFs, which are cheap in any implementation. It is about resampling. When a particle is selected three times, the naive implementation deep-copies its map three times, so each resampling step costs $O(MN)$ and a 100-particle filter with a 1,000-tree map copies 100,000 landmark filters every time $N_\text{eff}$ dips.

Montemerlo et al. avoided the copies by storing each particle's landmarks in a balanced binary tree keyed by landmark index [@Montemerlo2002FastSLAM]. A resampled particle starts out as a pointer to its parent's tree. Updating landmark $j$ copies only the $O(\log N)$ nodes on the path from the root to $j$ and shares every other subtree with the parent, so a scan costs $O(M \log N)$ instead of $O(MN)$. That logarithm is what let FastSLAM scale, in simulation, to maps with tens of thousands of landmarks, far beyond what a dense covariance allowed at the time.

In Python, the cheap and nearly-as-good version is **copy-on-write**. Treat each `LandmarkEKF` as an immutable value (`updated()` returns a new object; nothing ever modifies one in place), and copy a particle by making a new dictionary that points at the same landmark objects. Copying a dictionary is still $O(N)$, but it copies $N$ pointers rather than $2N$ NumPy arrays: on a typical laptop, copying a particle with 500 landmarks this way is about three orders of magnitude faster than `copy.deepcopy`. A persistent map, such as a hash array mapped trie, gives the true $O(\log N)$ behavior; it is not in the standard library, and for the project the dictionary is plenty.

## FastSLAM 2.0 {#sec-slam-fastslam2}

FastSLAM 1.0's proposal ignores the scan. When the sensor is much sharper than the odometry, most sampled poses land where the measurement likelihood is negligible, a handful of particles take all the weight, and resampling copies those few over and over until every particle shares the same recent history. This is the sample impoverishment of @sec-pf-sample-impoverishment, applied to whole paths. FastSLAM 2.0 [@Montemerlo2003FastSLAM2] instead samples each pose from a Gaussian approximation of the optimal proposal (@sec-pf-weighting), conditioned on the particle's own map and its association:

$$
\mathbf{x}_k^{[i]} \sim p\left(\mathbf{x}_k \mid \mathbf{x}_{k-1}^{[i]}, \mathbf{u}_k, \mathbf{z}_k, \mathbf{m}^{[i]}, n_k^{[i]}\right).
$$

Build it from two linearizations. The motion model gives a Gaussian prior for the new pose, $\mathbf{x}_k \sim \mathcal{N}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}, \mathbf{Q}_x)$, with $\bar{\mathbf{x}} = f(\mathbf{x}_{k-1}^{[i]}, \mathbf{u}_k)$ and pose-space process noise $\mathbf{Q}_x = \mathbf{L}\mathbf{Q}_u\mathbf{L}^T$. The measurement of the matched landmark, linearized in both the pose and the landmark and with the landmark integrated out, gives $\mathbf{z} \mid \mathbf{x}_k \sim \mathcal{N}\left(\hat{\mathbf{z}} + \mathbf{H}_x(\mathbf{x}_k - \bar{\mathbf{x}}),\ \mathbf{S}_\ell\right)$, where $\hat{\mathbf{z}} = h(\bar{\mathbf{x}}, \hat{\boldsymbol{\ell}}_j)$, $\mathbf{H}_x$ and $\mathbf{H}_\ell$ are the pose and landmark Jacobians, and $\mathbf{S}_\ell = \mathbf{H}_\ell \mathbf{P}_j \mathbf{H}_\ell^T + \mathbf{R}$ is the FastSLAM 1.0 innovation covariance. The product of the two Gaussians in $\mathbf{x}_k$ is the proposal:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_x &= \left(\mathbf{H}_x^T\mathbf{S}_\ell^{-1}\mathbf{H}_x + \mathbf{Q}_x^{-1}\right)^{-1}, \\
\boldsymbol{\mu}_x &= \bar{\mathbf{x}} + \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_x\mathbf{H}_x^T\mathbf{S}_\ell^{-1}\left(\mathbf{z} - \hat{\mathbf{z}}\right), \\
\mathbf{x}_k^{[i]} &\sim \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_x, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_x).
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-slam-fastslam2-proposal}

This is an EKF update of the pose that treats the landmark as a slightly fuzzy beacon. With the optimal proposal, the importance weight is the predictive likelihood of the measurement, which does not depend on the sampled pose:

$$
w_k^{[i]} \propto w_{k-1}^{[i]}\,
\mathcal{N}\left(\mathbf{z};\ \hat{\mathbf{z}},\ \mathbf{H}_x\mathbf{Q}_x\mathbf{H}_x^T + \mathbf{S}_\ell\right).
$$ {#eq-slam-fastslam2-weight}

Compared with @eq-slam-matched-weight, the only change is the extra $\mathbf{H}_x\mathbf{Q}_x\mathbf{H}_x^T$: the particle is judged before its pose is sampled, so the pose uncertainty belongs in the denominator.

::: {.callout-warning title="The literature swaps R and Q"}
Montemerlo et al. and Thrun, Burgard, and Fox [@Montemerlo2003FastSLAM2; @ProbRob] write the same equations with $\mathbf{R}$ for the motion noise and $\mathbf{Q}$ for the measurement (plus landmark) covariance, the reverse of this book's letters, and with their own names for the Jacobians. In this book $\mathbf{Q}$ is always process noise and $\mathbf{R}$ is always measurement noise. Translate before you copy.
:::

Four practical points turn the equations into code:

- For a unicycle with two noisy inputs, $\mathbf{Q}_x = \mathbf{L}\mathbf{Q}_u\mathbf{L}^T$ is $3 \times 3$ with rank 2, so $\mathbf{Q}_x^{-1}$ does not exist. Use the equivalent Kalman form, which the matrix inversion lemma guarantees: $\mathbf{K} = \mathbf{Q}_x\mathbf{H}_x^T(\mathbf{H}_x\mathbf{Q}_x\mathbf{H}_x^T + \mathbf{S}_\ell)^{-1}$, $\boldsymbol{\mu}_x = \bar{\mathbf{x}} + \mathbf{K}(\mathbf{z} - \hat{\mathbf{z}})$, $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_x = (\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{K}\mathbf{H}_x)\mathbf{Q}_x$.
- A scan with several matched observations is folded in one observation at a time, each update starting from the previous $(\boldsymbol{\mu}_x, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_x)$ and contributing its own factor @eq-slam-fastslam2-weight. The product of those factors is the joint predictive likelihood of the scan.
- Association is decided before sampling, at $\bar{\mathbf{x}}$, using the covariance $\mathbf{H}_x\mathbf{Q}_x\mathbf{H}_x^T + \mathbf{S}_\ell$ that includes the pose uncertainty, with the same two gates and mutual exclusion as before. A new or discarded observation says nothing about the pose, leaves the proposal alone, and is charged $p_0$.
- After sampling the pose, the landmark updates are exactly those of FastSLAM 1.0.

Montemerlo et al. prove that in the linear-Gaussian SLAM case FastSLAM 2.0 converges to the correct map even with a single particle, $M = 1$ [@Montemerlo2003FastSLAM2]. FastSLAM 1.0 has no such guarantee, and it is easy to see why: with $M = 1$, FastSLAM 1.0 is dead reckoning with a map attached, because a single particle drawn from the motion model never uses a measurement to correct its pose.

``` {.python .cell-code}
def control_jacobian(pose, control, dt, step=1e-6):
    """L = df/du for the unicycle model, by central differences."""
    L = np.zeros((3, 2))
    for k in range(2):
        du = np.zeros(2)
        du[k] = step
        diff = predict_pose(pose, control + du, dt) - predict_pose(pose, control - du, dt)
        diff[2] = wrap_angle(diff[2])
        L[:, k] = diff / (2.0 * step)
    return L


def pose_jacobian(H_l):
    """H_x = dh/d(pose) for range-bearing: [-H_l, (0, -1)^T]."""
    return np.hstack([-H_l, np.array([[0.0], [-1.0]])])


class FastSLAM2(FastSLAM):
    """FastSLAM 2.0: sample each pose from a Gaussian proposal that sees the scan."""

    def step(self, control, dt, scan):
        self.scan_index += 1
        for particle in self.particles:
            x_bar = predict_pose(particle.pose, control, dt)
            L = control_jacobian(particle.pose, control, dt)
            Sigma = L @ self.control_covariance @ L.T          # Q_x, rank 2

            # Associate at the predicted mean, with the pose uncertainty in S.
            ids = list(particle.landmarks)
            d2 = np.empty((len(scan), len(ids)))
            for col, j in enumerate(ids):
                lm = particle.landmarks[j]
                z_hat, H_l = lm.expected_measurement(x_bar)
                H_x = pose_jacobian(H_l)
                S_full = H_x @ Sigma @ H_x.T + H_l @ lm.covariance @ H_l.T + self.R
                for a, z in enumerate(scan):
                    nu = z - z_hat
                    nu[1] = wrap_angle(nu[1])
                    d2[a, col] = nu @ np.linalg.solve(S_full, nu)
            decisions = two_gate_decisions(
                d2, ids, self.associate_gate, self.birth_gate, self.mutual_exclusion
            )

            # Fold matched observations into the proposal one at a time (Kalman
            # form, so the rank-deficient Q_x is never inverted), and weight.
            x_hat = x_bar.copy()
            for z, j in zip(scan, decisions):
                if j in (NEW, DISCARD):
                    particle.log_weight += self.log_p0
                    continue
                lm = particle.landmarks[j]
                z_hat, H_l = lm.expected_measurement(x_hat)
                H_x = pose_jacobian(H_l)
                S_full = H_x @ Sigma @ H_x.T + H_l @ lm.covariance @ H_l.T + self.R
                nu = z - z_hat
                nu[1] = wrap_angle(nu[1])
                particle.log_weight += gaussian_log_likelihood(nu, S_full)
                K = np.linalg.solve(S_full, H_x @ Sigma).T
                x_hat = x_hat + K @ nu
                x_hat[2] = wrap_angle(x_hat[2])
                Sigma = (np.eye(3) - K @ H_x) @ Sigma
                Sigma = 0.5 * (Sigma + Sigma.T)

            # Sample the pose, then update the landmarks exactly as in 1.0.
            pose = self.rng.multivariate_normal(x_hat, Sigma)
            pose[2] = wrap_angle(pose[2])
            particle.pose = pose
            particle.trajectory.append(pose)
            for z, j in zip(scan, decisions):
                if j == NEW:
                    particle.landmarks[self.next_landmark_id] = LandmarkEKF.initialize(
                        pose, z, self.R, self.scan_index
                    )
                    self.next_landmark_id += 1
                elif j != DISCARD:
                    particle.landmarks[j] = particle.landmarks[j].updated(
                        pose, z, self.R, self.scan_index
                    )
            self._delete_stale_tentative(particle)
        self._finish_update()
```

## FastSLAM 1.0 vs. FastSLAM 2.0 {#sec-slam-fastslam-1-0}

FastSLAM 1.0 samples pose from the motion model,
$\mathbf{x}_k^{[i]} \sim p(\mathbf{x}_k \mid \mathbf{x}_{k-1}^{[i]}, \mathbf{u}_k)$;
FastSLAM 2.0 samples from @eq-slam-fastslam2-proposal, which also sees $\mathbf{z}_k$. On the toy world above, where the sensor is not much sharper than the odometry, the two behave about the same. The difference appears when the sensor is precise and the odometry is sloppy, which describes a lidar on a skid-steer robot, or a ship's radar fixing on charted buoys while the log and a magnetic compass do their best. ## GraphSLAM in One Page {#sec-slam-graphslam-one-page}

GraphSLAM treats poses and landmarks as variables in a nonlinear least-squares problem. The Durrant-Whyte and Bailey tutorial is a good high-level bridge between the filtering and graph views of SLAM [@DurrantWhyteBailey2006SLAMTutorial]:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\hat{\mathbf{X}} &= \arg\min_{\mathbf{X}} \sum_i \left\|\mathbf{e}_i(\mathbf{X})\right\|_{\boldsymbol{\Omega}_i}^2, \\
\|\mathbf{e}\|_{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}^2 &= \mathbf{e}^T\boldsymbol{\Omega}\,\mathbf{e}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Each residual $\mathbf{e}_i$ comes from a motion constraint, landmark observation, GPS prior, loop closure, or other measurement, and $\boldsymbol{\Omega}_i$ is its information matrix, the inverse of that measurement's covariance (@sec-information-filter). Minimizing the weighted squared residuals is maximum-likelihood estimation under Gaussian noise. The graph is sparse because each measurement touches only a few variables.

This is the dominant style in many modern systems:

- pose graph optimization for loop closure;
- bundle adjustment for visual SLAM;
- factor graphs in libraries such as GTSAM, Ceres, and g2o.

GraphSLAM handles loop closure naturally because past poses remain variables, and every iteration relinearizes them at the current best estimate. Filters marginalize the past instead. EKF-SLAM keeps the past's influence in its covariance and does propagate a loop correction through the whole map, but it cannot go back and relinearize old poses, so linearization errors made early are baked in. FastSLAM keeps whole paths, but only the ones its particles still carry; if resampling has already discarded the history that the loop closure needs, it is gone.

## Comparison for the Project Report {#sec-slam-comparison-project-report}

| Aspect | EKF-SLAM | FastSLAM | GraphSLAM |
|---|---|---|---|
| State representation | one joint Gaussian | particles plus landmark EKFs | graph of variables and factors |
| Landmark correlations | explicit dense covariance | conditional independence per particle | implicit through graph solution |
| Data association | one decision per measurement | per-particle hypotheses | front-end plus robust optimization |
| Loop closure | correction propagates through the correlations; limited by $O(N^2)$ cost and linearization overconfidence | possible, if a particle with the right history survived | natural: the trajectory is re-solved |
| Scaling concern | $O(N^2)$ per update and in memory | particle count; map copies ($O(M \log N)$ with sharing) | sparse linear algebra |

## Practical Failure Modes {#sec-slam-practical-failure-modes}

FastSLAM fails in recognizable ways:

- **Particle depletion:** too few particles survive after repeated informative measurements; $N_\text{eff}$ stays low and resampling fires at nearly every scan.
- **Path degeneracy:** even with healthy $N_\text{eff}$, repeated resampling leaves every particle descended from one ancestor a few dozen scans back. Bailey, Nieto, and Nebot showed that this makes FastSLAM 1.0 inconsistent over long runs no matter how many particles it uses [@bailey2006fastslam]; the ancestor count in @sec-slam-fastslam-1-0 shows it happening.
- **Duplicate landmarks:** the gate is too tight, the pose uncertainty is too large, $p_0$ is missing, or one gate is doing the work of two.
- **Merged landmarks:** the gate is too loose or measurement covariance is too optimistic.
- **Outlier landmarks:** moving objects, non-tree returns, or bad segmentation are accepted; the tentative stage exists to keep them out of the reported map.
- **Delayed loop closure:** the correct revisited-place hypothesis may no longer exist in the particle set.

The cure is not one magic parameter. It is measurement modeling, feature filtering, enough particles, careful resampling, and diagnostic plots.

## Summary {#sec-slam-summary}

EKF-SLAM teaches why landmark correlations matter and what they cost. GraphSLAM teaches why sparse optimization dominates many modern systems. FastSLAM is the implementation target because it sits directly between the particle filters students already know and the landmark-based Victoria Park dataset.

For the project, the expected backend is:

1. sample particle poses from odometry (FastSLAM 1.0);
2. maintain per-particle landmark EKFs (2-D mean, $2 \times 2$ covariance);
3. associate per particle with two gates (5.99 to match, 13.82 to spawn), mutual exclusion, and tentative/confirmed tracks;
4. weight with $\log \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\nu}; \mathbf{0}, \mathbf{S})$ for matches and $\log p_0$ otherwise, normalized with log-sum-exp;
5. resample systematically when $N_\text{eff} < M/2$;
6. report both map quality and failure modes.
